questions.stem: What ion does a halogen atom form when it reacts?

options.text: A -1 ion called a halide ion
options.explanation: Gaining the single missing electron gives the completed outer shell one extra negative charge, so the ion is a 1- halide.

options.text: A +1 ion, formed by losing the outer electron
options.explanation: That is the Group 1 pattern; halogens sit one column left of a full shell, so they gain rather than lose.

options.text: A -7 ion, one charge per outer electron
options.explanation: Only the single vacancy in the outer shell is filled, so the ion carries a single negative charge.
options.misconception: outer-electron count read as the ion charge

options.text: No ion forms, because halogens share electrons only
options.explanation: Halogens do form covalent molecules with non-metals, but with metals and in displacement chemistry the 1- halide ion is standard.

questions.stem: Which statement gives the reactivity trend down Group 7 correctly?

options.text: Reactivity decreases as you go down the group
options.explanation: Fluorine is the fiercest halogen and iodine the mildest of the three tested, so reactivity falls with depth.

options.text: Reactivity increases as you go down the group
options.explanation: That is the Group 1 trend; Group 7 runs the opposite way because it gains electrons instead of losing them.

options.text: All halogens react with equal vigour
options.explanation: Their displacement chemistry and hydrogen reactions clearly differ in vigour down the group.

options.text: Reactivity peaks in the middle of the group at bromine
options.explanation: There is no peak; the trend runs steadily from the highly reactive top of the group to the sluggish bottom.

questions.stem: Why is fluorine the most reactive halogen?

options.text: Its outermost shell is the closest to the positive nucleus, so it attracts the gained electron most strongly
options.explanation: With the fewest shells, fluorine's incoming electron feels the strongest pull, which makes its electron gain the easiest and fastest.

options.text: It has the most electron shells, so it has the most room for electrons
options.explanation: Fluorine has the fewest shells; the strong pull comes from the short distance, not from extra room.

options.text: It is the lightest halogen, so it moves fastest
options.explanation: Mass and speed are not the drivers; reactivity tracks the strength of attraction for the gained electron.

options.text: It is the most abundant halogen in the laboratory
options.explanation: Availability has nothing to do with the position of fluorine at the top of the reactivity trend.

questions.stem: How does the force of attraction between the nucleus and the outermost shell change down Group 7?

options.text: It decreases, because the outermost shell sits further from the nucleus
options.explanation: Each extra shell adds distance, and electrostatic attraction weakens with distance, so the outer electrons feel less pull.

options.text: It increases, because the nucleus holds more protons
options.explanation: Although the proton count rises, the added shells increase the distance further, and distance wins the comparison.

options.text: It stays the same across the group
options.explanation: A constant attraction would give constant electron-gain ease, contradicting the clear reactivity trend.

options.text: It disappears entirely for the largest halogens
options.explanation: Attraction weakens but never vanishes; even iodine still draws in an electron, just less keenly.

questions.stem: A student says iodine is more reactive than chlorine because its atoms are bigger. What is the correct verdict?

options.text: Wrong: the bigger atom's outer shell is further from the nucleus, so gaining an electron is harder and iodine is less reactive
options.explanation: Size here means distance, and distance weakens the pull on the incoming electron, placing iodine below chlorine in reactivity.

options.text: Correct: bigger atoms always react faster
options.explanation: For halogens the reverse holds; extra shells distance the outer shell and weaken the electron gain.

options.text: Correct, but only when the iodine is dissolved
options.explanation: Solution state does not reverse the group trend; iodine is the weaker electron-gainer in every state.

options.text: The claim cannot be judged without displacement data
options.explanation: The electronic configuration explanation alone settles it, which is exactly what the specification asks you to apply.

questions.stem: What ion do halogen atoms form when they react, and what is its charge called?
questions.modelAnswer: A halogen atom gains one electron during reactions to form a -1 ion called a halide ion.

questions.stem: Which halogen is the most reactive of the group, and what atomic feature makes it so?
questions.modelAnswer: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen in the group because it has the smallest atom.

questions.stem: Explain why the reactivity of the Group 7 non-metals falls on descending the group.
questions.modelAnswer: The number of electron shells increases by one with each element down the group, so the outer shell lies further from the nucleus; the growing distance weakens the attraction for the electron being gained, making it harder to gain and lowering the reactivity.

questions.stem: Astatine sits below iodine in Group 7. Predict whether astatine reacts more or less readily than iodine, and state how many electrons one astatine atom gains when it reacts.
questions.modelAnswer: Astatine reacts less readily than iodine, because reactivity decreases down the group; each astatine atom gains one electron to form a -1 halide ion.

questions.stem: How many electrons does each Group 7 atom carry in its outermost shell?

options.text: Seven
options.explanation: Seven outer electrons leave each halogen exactly one short of a noble gas arrangement, which drives the electron gain.

options.text: One
options.explanation: One outer electron belongs to Group 1; the halogens carry seven and gain one more.

options.text: Eight
options.explanation: Eight outer electrons is the complete noble gas set; halogens reach it only after gaining one electron.
options.misconception: completed shell credited before the gain

options.text: It varies from seven down to one through the group
options.explanation: The outer count is fixed at seven for the whole group; what varies is the number of inner shells.
options.misconception: outer count thought to drift down the group

questions.stem: What changes in the atom as you move from chlorine to bromine to iodine?

options.text: One more filled inner shell at each step, so the outer shell lies further out
options.explanation: Each element down the group occupies the next period, adding a complete shell and enlarging the atom.

options.text: The outer shell count falls from seven towards five
options.explanation: The outer count stays at seven; only the total number of shells grows.

options.text: The nucleus shrinks, pulling everything closer
options.explanation: Nuclei grow with proton count down the group; it is the shell distance that increases.

options.text: Nothing changes, so all three behave identically
options.explanation: Reactions are similar in type but differ in vigour, precisely because of the added shells.
options.misconception: similarity of pattern read as identity

questions.stem: Why does the increased distance from the outer shell to the nucleus make halogens less reactive down the group?

options.text: The pull on the electron to be gained is weaker, so gaining it is harder
options.explanation: Reactivity for a halogen means attracting one electron; weaker pull at distance means slower, less vigorous reactions.

options.text: The atoms become too heavy to move towards the metal
options.explanation: Movement of whole atoms is irrelevant; the trend lives in the attraction for a single electron.

options.text: The outer shells of different atoms can no longer touch
options.explanation: Contact between reactants is not the limiting factor; the strength of the electron gain is.

options.text: Larger atoms can hold more than one extra electron
options.explanation: Halogens gain exactly one electron to fill the shell; capacity does not change the trend.

questions.stem: Which comparison between fluorine and iodine is correct?

options.text: Fluorine attracts an extra electron more strongly and is the more reactive halogen
options.explanation: Fluorine's short distance to the nucleus gives the strongest pull, so its electron gain is easiest and its reactions fiercest.

options.text: Iodine attracts an extra electron more strongly because it has more protons
options.explanation: The extra protons of iodine are offset by much greater distance; the net pull is weaker, not stronger.

options.text: Both attract electrons equally, differing only in colour
options.explanation: Their displacement chemistry shows the difference plainly: fluorine would displace iodide instantly, iodine displaces nothing.

options.text: Iodine is more reactive because it is a solid
options.explanation: Physical state follows the intermolecular trend and has no bearing on electron gain.

questions.stem: In an exam answer on the Group 7 trend, which chain of reasoning is complete and correct?

options.text: More shells down the group, greater distance, weaker attraction for the gained electron, lower reactivity
options.explanation: This chain runs from configuration to reactivity in the direction the trend actually flows, which earns the full explanation mark.

options.text: More protons, stronger attraction, higher reactivity down the group
options.explanation: That chain predicts the Group 1 direction; for Group 7 the distance effect dominates and reactivity falls.

options.text: Heavier molecules, more collisions, faster reactions
options.explanation: Collision counting does not describe a single atom's electron gain, which is what the trend measures.

options.text: Larger atoms, more shells, easier electron loss
options.explanation: Halogens gain electrons; describing loss describes Group 1 and inverts the explanation.
options.misconception: gain and loss swapped in the chain

questions.stem: State the number of outer-shell electrons shared by every Group 7 atom.
questions.modelAnswer: All Group 7 atoms have seven electrons in their outermost shell.

questions.stem: Going from chlorine to bromine to iodine, what is added to the atom at each step?
questions.modelAnswer: One filled shell is added at each element, so the number of shells rises by one on descending the group.

questions.stem: Explain why gaining an electron becomes harder for the halogens as the group is descended.
questions.modelAnswer: The added shells carry the outermost shell further from the nucleus, so the attraction between the nucleus and the incoming electron grows weaker with distance, and gaining that electron becomes harder, so reactivity falls.

questions.stem: Chlorine's outer shell occupies period 3 while bromine's occupies period 4. Using this lesson's distance law, predict which atom attracts an incoming electron more strongly and name the more reactive halogen of the pair.
questions.modelAnswer: Chlorine attracts the incoming electron more strongly: its outer shell is one shell closer to the nucleus, so the attraction is greater and the electron is easier to gain, making chlorine the more reactive halogen.
